title: Backport an entire feature that arrived as a merge
summary: The fix you need is not one commit — it is a merge of three. Cherry-pick the merge commit itself with -m, and compare that against picking the commits individually.
mental_model: A merge commit has no single diff — it has one per parent. `-m 1` tells cherry-pick to use the diff against the first parent, which is 'everything the merged branch brought in', flattened into one commit.

steps.title: Find the merge you need
steps.why: The retry helper reached main as a three-commit branch behind a merge commit. Customers on release/1.0 need the whole feature, not one of its commits.
steps.expect: A merge commit with two parents.

steps.title: Watch cherry-pick refuse
steps.why: Same reason as revert: a merge has two diffs and git will not guess which one you mean. The error names the flag you need.
steps.expect: error: commit ... is a merge but no -m option was given.

steps.title: Pick it against the first parent
steps.why: `-m 1` uses the diff between the merge and main-before-the-merge — that is, everything the feature branch contributed. The result is one commit on the release branch containing the whole feature.
steps.expect: One new commit, all three files' worth of change flattened into it.

verify.label: …as a single commit on the release branch

steps.title: Confirm nothing unrelated came with it
steps.why: The commit after the merge stayed on main. Cherry-picking the merge brings the feature and only the feature — which is exactly what a patch release needs.

verify.label: main's later work was not dragged along

steps.title: The alternative: pick the commits individually
steps.why: Picking the range keeps the three commits distinct, which preserves reviewability and lets `git bisect` work inside the feature. It costs three conflict resolutions instead of one.
steps.expect: Three commits instead of one, same resulting files.

verify.label: the granular backport kept each commit separate
verify.hint: git cherry-pick <merge>^1..<merge>^2 picks the branch's own commits

steps.title: Compare the two results
steps.why: Identical trees, different histories. Flattened is quicker and reads as one release note; granular is better if you may need to bisect or revert part of it later.

verify.label: both approaches produce the same code

steps.title: Ship the flattened one
steps.why: For a patch release, one commit describing one feature is usually the right trade. Tag it and the backport is done.
commands: git tag -a v1.0.1 -m "Patch release 1.0.1 — backport retry helper"

verify.label: and nothing unrelated came with it
it landed as one flattened commit
the granular backport produced identical code

pitfalls: `-m 1` is the mainline parent — the branch that was merged INTO. `-m 2` gives you the inverse diff and almost never what you want.
A flattened merge loses the individual commit messages. Write a good message on the pick, because the detail is gone.
`<merge>^1..<merge>^2` is the idiom for 'the commits the branch contributed'. Read it as: everything in the second parent that is not in the first.
If the feature depends on something else on main, neither approach will apply cleanly. Backport the dependency first.
